title: Elastic shape coalescer and priority-decay scheduling (design notes)
content:
Overview

Problem statement
Many real-world inference workloads produce highly skewed sequence lengths within short windows: short system prompts, medium user prompts, and long contextual histories. Naive global padding wastes tokens; rigid bucketing increases latency for deadline-sensitive requests. We need a lightweight runtime strategy that reduces padding waste while preserving tail latency SLOs and allowing kernel selection to target the best execution path for each micro-batch.

Goal
Design an elastic shape coalescer that incrementally forms micro-batches across a short time window, coalesces shapes when beneficial, and applies a priority-decay scheduling policy so deadline-sensitive requests are favored but not starved. The design must include:
- a deterministic micro-batch assembly algorithm
- latency-aware kernel selection rules (fast-path vs segmented kernels)
- KV cache tagging and sharing semantics across quantization or kernel variants
- metrics and backstop fallbacks for SLO violations

Key ideas and intuition
1) Progressive coalescing: instead of assigning a request immediately to a pre-made bucket, we briefly hold incoming requests for up to T_hold ms (10-40 ms tuning param) and form a micro-batch that groups similar lengths first but will accept length diversity if it increases GPU occupancy. The hold window is bounded by per-request deadline metadata.

2) Priority-decay scheduling: each request arrives with an initial priority derived from its deadline slack and customer tier. If a request waits, its priority decays slowly to avoid indefinite starvation of low-priority but long requests. Decay curve is configurable (linear/exponential). Scheduling chooses the highest-priority micro-batch ready to dispatch.

3) Elastic padding with 2-stage execution: for micro-batches with small length variance, use the contiguous fast-path kernel (single padded sequence). For high variance, split execution into two stages: stage A executes the first L_shared tokens with a contiguous kernel to maximize utilization, stage B executes tails using a segmented/gather-scatter kernel that only touches remaining positions. This reduces total padded token count compared to single-stage padding to max length.

4) KV cache tagging for compatibility: requests carry a KV compatibility tag encoding model version, quantization format, and kernel ABI. The KV cache is partitioned by tag; we allow cross-tag reuse only if a compatibility shim exists (e.g., same model weights but different quantization can share decoded keys on-the-fly with a conversion cost). Eviction policies prefer keeping frequently reused prefixes across tags where conversion cost is low.

Algorithm sketch: elastic coalescer
- On request arrival, compute deadline_slack = deadline_timestamp - now and initial_priority = f(deadline_slack, customer_tier). Attach shape = seq_len.
- Place request in pending pool; attempt immediate placement in existing micro-batch with shape distance metric D = alpha * abs(len - mean_len) + beta * quantization_mismatch_penalty. If D < threshold, append.
- If no matching micro-batch, open a new micro-batch and start a hold timer. Each micro-batch has an earliest_dispatch_by = min(request.deadline) - min_latency_buffer.
- Micro-batches are eligible for dispatch when any of: hold timer expires, batch size reaches target, or the earliest_dispatch_by is reached. At dispatch time, compute shape variance and choose kernel path: contiguous if variance < V_thresh and estimated padded_tokens cost < segmented_cost_estimate; otherwise elastic 2-stage.

Kernel selection and cost model
We use a simple cost heuristic to choose execution path: Estimated_cost_contiguous = O1 * padded_tokens + O2 * kernel_launch_overhead. Estimated_cost_segmented = O3 * shared_tokens + O4 * tail_tokens + O5 * gather_scatter_penalty. Constants O1..O5 are calibrated from microbenchmarks per model and hardware. The coalescer queries a local performance profile to get those constants.

KV cache semantics and coordination
- KV entries are keyed by (request_prefix_hash, model_version, quant_tag).
- On stage A execution when multiple requests share a common prefix, we attempt to reuse a single KV write and then clone pointers into per-request contexts to avoid duplication on-device.
- Conversion shim: when quant_tag differs but model_version is identical, we allow lazy conversion at read time if conversion_cost < read_miss_penalty. Conversion happens on a small conversion workspace to avoid interfering with main cache space.

Priority decay and starvation protection
- Priority_i(t) = initial_priority_i * decay_func(wait_time_i). decay_func can be 1 / (1 + lambda * wait_time) for soft decay or exp(-lambda * wait_time) for aggressive decay. We cap wait_time at a configured max so priorities don't collapse to zero.
- Starvation protection rule: any request older than Starve_threshold automatically promoted and will be included in next dispatch regardless of D.

Metrics to observe
- padded_token_ratio (tokens produced vs effective consumed tokens) over time windows
- tail_p95/p99 latency per customer_tier and per model
- micro-batch degree_of_variance distribution
- kernel_choice_ratio (contiguous vs elastic vs segmented) and per-choice per-token throughput
- KV hit rate by tag and cross-tag conversion counts and conversion latency

Expected benefits and tradeoffs
- Reduced padded tokens for mixed-length traffic (expect 8-30% token savings vs greedy global padding, depends on workload).
- Slight additional scheduling CPU overhead and micro-batching latency (bounded by T_hold).
- Additional complexity around KV conversion and bookkeeping; conversion costs must be measured and bounded.

Implementation plan and milestones
1) Bench infra: add microbench harness that measures O1..O5 for representative models and GPUs (PR 2789 covers part of this).
2) Scheduler prototype: implement pending pool and D-based matching, simple hold timer, and priority decay hooks. Feature-flag behind elastic_coalescer_v1.
3) Kernel orchestration: implement contiguous and simple 2-stage segmented execution path inside runtime; add per-batch execution planner that emits stage boundaries.
4) KV tagging and shim: add tag metadata, partitioned cache store, and conversion shim prototype; guard with config enablement.
5) Canary experiments: run internal canary on staging region, collect metrics, tune thresholds.

Open questions and risks
- How to set thresholds for D and V_thresh across diverse workloads? Recommend an automated tuning job that explores parameter space per-customer.
- Conversion cost variability across GPUs and quant formats might exceed expected budget, causing SLO regressions. Need conservative default: disallow cross-tag conversion until measured.
- Memory fragmentation when cloning KV pointers for stage A optimization. We should prefer pointer aliasing and refcounts instead of physical copies.

Appendix: simple pseudocode for dispatcher loop
for each incoming request r:
  annotate priority and tag
  try append to best_batch by minimizing D(batch, r)
  if appended: continue
  else open new batch and start hold timer

periodic tick:
  eligible_batches = batches where hold_timer expired or size >= min_target or earliest_dispatch_by reached
  sort eligible_batches by max_priority_in_batch descending
  for batch in eligible_batches:
    if kernel_choice(batch) == contiguous:
      dispatch_contiguous(batch)
    else:
      dispatch_elastic_two_stage(batch)

Notes for next iteration
- Consider integrating prediction of future arrivals using short-term arrival-rate model to further reduce hold latency when traffic is sparse.
- Evaluate combining with prefix clustering for KV sharing when histories align.

End of notes
